cues.en: So I'm Chandler Carruth. I work at Google on C++ and LLVM and compilers and performance and a bunch of other stuff. And I'm here to give a talk today because I feel bad, actually. I think I've been at CppCon in the past and I've talked about zero cost abstractions. I may have even advocated that you all should use zero cost abstractions. These are good things and that C++ is great because it gives them to us. But today I'm here to kind of apologize and say that I was wrong.
cues.zh: 大家好，我是 Chandler Carruth。我在 Google 从事 C++、LLVM、编译器、性能优化等相关工作。今天我来做这个演讲，其实是因为我心里有点愧疚。之前参加 CppCon 时，我曾大谈零成本抽象（zero cost abstractions）。甚至可能还鼓吹过大家都应该用零成本抽象，说这是好东西，C++ 之所以伟大就是因为它为我们提供了这些。但今天我是来向大家道歉的，我想说：我错了。

cues.en: A lot of other people were wrong. And in fact, there are no zero cost abstractions. And imagining that there are is causing us serious problems. And so that's going to be the theme of this talk is, why do abstractions have cost? What problems does that cause for us? And how do we want to cope with that reality? So with that, let's start going here by thinking a little bit about what abstractions we really care about in C++. What do we mean when we talk about abstractions in C++ code?
cues.zh: 很多人也错了。事实上，根本就不存在零成本抽象。妄想它们存在，反而给我们带来了严重的问题。这就是本次演讲的主题：为什么抽象是有成本的？这给我们带来了什么问题？以及我们该如何面对这个现实？那么，让我们先来思考一下：在 C++ 中，我们真正关心的究竟是哪些抽象？当我们谈论 C++ 代码中的抽象时，到底是指什么？

cues.en: We'll start with the very simple, the very fundamental abstractions, the easy to use hammer that doesn't take a lot of work, but it's probably more effective than trying to push a nail in with your hand. Still, it's useful. We have functions. Functions work pretty well as abstractions. We can have loops to do things multiple times over some data structures. These are great abstractions that we can use.
cues.zh: 我们先从最简单、最基础的抽象讲起。就像一把顺手的小锤子，用起来不费劲，但肯定比徒手往里按钉子管用得多，非常实用。比如函数，函数就是一种很好用的抽象；我们还有循环，可以对某些数据结构反复执行操作。这些都是我们可以使用的绝佳抽象。

cues.en: We can have memory, right? We can have pointers into memory. Memory is a fantastic abstraction to use in C++. Allows us to take the lifetime of objects and move them out of lexical scopes and do all kinds of other wonderful things. These are also really fundamental abstractions. Almost every language has them. We know about them really well. We expect every program to use them. These probably aren't the primary problems. Let's talk about C++. C++ brings us an important...
cues.zh: 我们还可以操作内存，对吧？我们有指向内存的指针。在 C++ 里，内存是一个极好的抽象。它允许我们将对象的生命周期移出词法作用域，还能做各种奇妙的事情。这些也是极其基础的抽象，几乎每门语言都有，我们对它们了如指掌，也理所当然地认为每个程序都会用到。这些大概不是最主要的问题所在。让我们来聊聊 C++，C++ 为我们带来了一个重要的……

cues.en: The baseline abstraction level, your typical work hammer to get things done in C++ is the type. Everyone has types, these are great abstractions. We even have more powerful abstractions in C++. Really powerful ones. Kind of like a sledgehammer that can actually do some good work here. We have templates, and templates are really, really cool and really powerful. I love templates. We even have bigger sledgehammers.
cues.zh: 基准抽象层次，在 C++ 里用来干活的典型铁锤，就是类型（type）。人人都会用到类型，这是极好的抽象。在 C++ 中我们甚至还有更强大的抽象，非常强悍。就像一把真正能派上大用场的大铁锤。我们有模板（templates），模板简直酷毙了，而且威力无穷。我超爱模板。但我们甚至还有更大的铁锤。

cues.en: we have metaprogramming in C++, and it's awesome. You can do amazing things with it. We don't just have metaprogramming. We have two different metaprogramming systems in C++, and you can even sometimes use them together. And so that's really great. These are powerful abstractions. We get a lot done with these. I don't even think these are the most powerful, though. I think that there's an even more powerful abstraction that we tend to use in C++, at least in my code base. At Google, we use this very, very often.
cues.zh: 在 C++ 里我们有元编程（metaprogramming），太棒了，你可以用它做出惊人的事情。而且我们不仅有元编程，C++ 里甚至有两套不同的元编程体系，有时候你还能把它们混着用。这简直太棒了。这些都是强大的抽象，帮我们搞定了很多事情。不过，我甚至觉得这些都还算不上最强大的。我认为在 C++ 中，我们往往还会用到一种更强大的抽象，至少在我的代码库里是这样。在 Google，我们非常非常频繁地使用它。

cues.en: It's kind of like the largest hammer you could ever imagine. It can do anything, but it's actually not C++ in most cases. It's usually a Python script that generates C++ at build time, and often a lot of C++ and often really complex C++. Of course, this is more powerful than all the others because I can generate all of the other abstractions from my Python script and use them. Okay, so those are abstractions. But what do we mean by cost? What is the cost of an abstraction?
cues.zh: 它就像你能想象到的最大的一把锤子。它什么都能干，但大多数情况下其实不是 C++。通常是一个 Python 脚本，在构建时生成 C++，而且往往生成很多 C++，还经常是特别复杂的 C++。当然，它比其他所有方式都更强大，因为我可以从 Python 脚本里生成其他所有抽象，然后把它们用起来。好，那些就是抽象。但我们说的成本是什么意思？一个抽象的成本是什么？

cues.en: And we can break this down into a few areas. The primary cost is going to be runtime, but we also want to think about build time and human time cost. Now, runtime, we understand. If you use too many abstractions, everything slows down. Your whole program feels laggy and slow and weird, and it's really frustrating. Almost as frustrating as the DMV. But build time, of course, we typify with compiling, right? We have the best XKCD comment for compiling.
cues.zh: 我们可以把它拆成几个方面。主要成本会是运行时，但我们也得考虑构建时间和人的时间成本。运行时我们懂。抽象用得太多，所有东西都会变慢。整个程序感觉卡顿、缓慢又别扭，真的很让人抓狂。几乎和去车管所一样抓狂。但构建时间嘛，当然，我们通常用编译来代表，对吧？关于编译，我们有最棒的 XKCD 吐槽。

cues.en: But build time is actually a much bigger space than that. It's not just about compiling. After they fight down the hallway one direction, they come back because they're still linking. And at least in my code base, even after they come back from linking, they still have to load all of the dynamic libraries to run the test. And that's also really slow. So there are a bunch of different things in the build space that add cost to our abstraction mechanisms.
cues.zh: 但构建时间其实是个大得多的空间。它不只是编译。它们沿着走廊朝一个方向打完，又回来了，因为还在链接。至少在我的代码库里，即使链接完回来，还得加载所有动态库才能跑测试。而那也很慢。所以构建这个空间里有一堆不同的东西，会给我们的抽象机制增加成本。

cues.en: And for humans, we also have costs, right? It takes a lot more of your brain to think about and work with complex abstractions. I mean, functions are pretty easy, but when you get to types and templates, much less generated code, it can be incredibly difficult to reason about how your code works with these abstractions. Okay? And these are real human costs of abstractions that we need to remember. Now, why aren't these costs zero? Why can't we get rid of these costs?
cues.zh: 对人来说，我们也有成本，对吧？思考和操作复杂抽象会占用你更多脑力。函数还挺简单，但到了类型和模板，更别说生成代码，要推理你的代码如何与这些抽象协作，会难到离谱。对吧？这些是抽象真实的人力成本，我们得记住。那么，为什么这些成本不是零？为什么我们不能把这些成本消掉？

cues.en: Fundamentally, we're doing work with the abstraction. We're getting some value out of it. It's doing work on our behalf so that we don't have to do it kind of manually and mechanically ourselves. And we do work, much like in physics, energy is required. And you can't make energy just go away. If anyone here has a perpetual motion machine, please let me know. No? OK. But energy just moves around. We can transfer it from one place to another.
cues.zh: 从根本上说，抽象是在替我们干活。我们从它那里得到一些价值。它在代表我们做事，这样我们就不必自己手动、机械地去做。而我们做事，就像物理里一样，需要能量。你没法让能量凭空消失。如果这里有谁有永动机，请告诉我。没有？好。但能量只是到处转移。我们可以把它从一个地方转移到另一个地方。

cues.en: But it doesn't go away, it doesn't ever vanish, and the cost of your abstractions don't either. And sometimes they can be really surprising. So, I wanna try and tell you three stories that I have about abstraction costs that were surprising, that we didn't really see coming. And the first of these stories is about a system that is really, really important to me. It's called protocol buffers. How many folks here have ever heard of protocol buffers? Wait, wait, you're clapping?
cues.zh: 但它不会消失，永远不会凭空不见，你那些抽象的成本也一样。而且有时候它们会非常出人意料。所以我想试着讲三个我遇到的抽象成本故事，它们都很出乎意料，我们当时真没预见到。第一个故事关于一个对我非常重要的系统。它叫 protocol buffers。这里有多少人听说过 protocol buffers？等等，等等，你们在鼓掌？

cues.en: But a lot of people know what protocol buffers are, which is good. It's good that we all know what protocol buffers are. At Google, at least, protocol buffers are kind of very fundamental. We solve everything at Google with protocol buffers. Want to build a storage system? We're going to use protocol buffers inside it. Want to do something? It's always going to be protocol buffers. Unfortunately, they also cause a lot of problems. Anything that becomes that ubiquitous causes a lot of problems. And one of the reasons they cause problems is that they're a code generator.
cues.zh: 但很多人都知道 protocol buffers 是什么，这很好，大家都了解它真是太棒了。至少在 Google，protocol buffers 是非常基础的核心技术。在 Google，我们用 protocol buffers 解决一切问题。想构建存储系统？我们底层会用 protocol buffers。想做点别的？到头来也全都是 protocol buffers。不幸的是，它们也引发了大量问题。任何变得如此普遍的东西都会带来很多麻烦。而它们引发问题的原因之一，就是它们本质上是个代码生成器。

cues.en: They're an incredibly big hammer. In fact, they're about the biggest hammer I know how to find. And so when we use protocol buffers, it's tended to come back and cause us some problems historically. But let's do a quick overview of what protocol buffers actually are and how they work. Protocol buffers let you define messages. We have two examples here. You can also put fields into them, like x and name. And you can even embed one message inside another.
cues.zh: 它们就像一把极其巨大的大锤。事实上，它们是我所知能找到的最大的一把锤子。所以从历史上看，我们使用 protocol buffers 时，往往反过来会遇到一些棘手问题。但我们还是快速回顾一下 protocol buffers 究竟是什么、以及它们是如何工作的吧。Protocol buffers 允许你定义消息（message）。我们这里有两个例子。你也可以在其中添加字段，比如 x 和 name。你甚至可以将一个消息嵌套在另一个消息中。

cues.en: And this basically lets you have nice descriptive data formats that you can serialize and deserialize, and we build a tremendous amount of our technology on top of these. And because of that nesting relationship, because you often will use one message and put it inside of another, maybe multiple messages and then those inside of still more, our protocol buffers tend to end up looking like some really high fan out graph.
cues.zh: 这基本上能让你拥有直观描述性强的数据格式，便于进行序列化和反序列化，我们的绝大部分技术都是构筑在它们之上的。由于这种嵌套关系，由于你经常会把一个消息放进另一个消息中，甚至套入多个消息，然后它们又被嵌进更多的消息里，我们的 protocol buffers 最终往往会呈现出一种扇出度极高的图结构。

cues.en: as you kind of mess things together into larger and larger messages, and you build out this complex data representation. Now, I said these are really fundamental at Google, and you may wonder, what are we doing with all of these protocol buffers? Well, we're moving them around. You see, we write servers, and they take protocol buffers in, and then they modify them slightly, and then they move them out into a response. And then they do that again and again. And so at Google, there's a common joke.
cues.zh: 随着你把各种东西混杂拼凑成越来越大的消息，你构建出了这种复杂的数据表示形式。之前我说过这在 Google 非常基础，你可能会好奇，我们拿这么多 protocol buffers 到底在干嘛呢？嗯，我们在倒腾它们。你看，我们编写各种服务器，它们接收 protocol buffers，做些微调，然后再打包进响应里发出去。接着一次又一次地重复这个过程。所以在 Google 有个常见的笑话：

cues.en: that all we really do is move protocol buffers around. And you can imagine what this looks like, right? You take some subgraph of your tree over here, and you're just going to re-parent it into some other part of the tree in order to update a message, in order to build a response from some request. Now, it turns out if that's all you do, it can get really expensive, okay? Because these are all objects, and they're very dynamic objects. There are a large number of heap allocations in here.
cues.zh: 我们其实整天就只是在到处倒腾 protocol buffers。你可以想象一下这看起来是什么样，对吧？你从这边的树里截取某个子图，然后把它重新挂载到树的另一部分，以此来更新消息，或者根据某个请求构建出响应。但事实证明，如果你整天只干这个，开销可能会变得非常大，懂吧？因为这些全都是对象，而且是非常动态的对象。这里面包含了大量的堆内存分配。

cues.en: But we also don't want to have too much fragmentation. So these aren't just tiny objects. They tend to have a little bit of aggregation in them. They tend to be fairly complex. We reuse them whenever it's possible. The requests that come in off of the network are often immutable. And so when we build a response, we might have to copy data into the response. Even if we're trying to move these protocol buffers around, we can end up doing a lot of work. So we wanted to optimize that.
cues.zh: 但我们又不想产生太多的内存碎片。所以它们可不只是微小的对象。它们内部往往包含了一定程度的聚合，结构往往相当复杂。只要有可能，我们就会复用它们。从网络进来的请求通常是不可变的。因此在我们构建响应时，可能必须把数据拷贝到响应中。哪怕我们只是想倒腾这些 protocol buffers，最终也可能会做大量的无用功。所以我们希望能优化这一点。

cues.en: There's a pretty good way of optimizing an allocation-heavy graph-like data structure when you're doing mutations on it. And that's by using arena-based allocation. So there's a project at Google a number of years back to add arena-based allocation to protocol buffers. We dug into the code that was generated for the protocol buffers, and we found where the moving of protocol buffers around was implemented. Now, unfortunately, protocol buffers predate C++ 11 at Google. And so all of our moving was actually implemented originally in terms of swap.
cues.zh: 当你在对分配密集型的图状数据结构做修改时，有一种非常好的优化方法。那就是使用基于 arena 的内存分配。几年前 Google 有个项目，旨在为 Protocol Buffers 引入基于 arena 的分配方式。我们深入研究了为 Protocol Buffers 生成的代码，找到了实现移动 Protocol Buffers 的地方。遗憾的是，Protocol Buffers 在 Google 的诞生早于 C++11。所以我们最初的所有移动操作，实际上都是基于 swap 来实现的。

cues.en: And if you remember from Titus' talk, or if you watch Titus' talk, he talks about how it's really difficult to refactor higher order abstractions. And the same way that it's more difficult to refactor a type than it is a function, it's even more difficult to refactor generated code in some cases. Okay, and so now we have generated types. And so even to this day, we still have swaps as the primary implementation strategy for our moves. Because reimagining all of this interface is so difficult.
cues.zh: 如果你还记得 Titus 的演讲，或者去看过他的演讲，他谈到了重构高阶抽象到底有多难。就像重构类型要比重构函数更困难一样，在某些情况下，重构生成的代码还要更难。好了，现在我们有了生成的类型。所以即使到了今天，swap 依然是我们实现移动操作的主要策略。因为要想重新构想这整套接口，实在是太难了。

cues.en: And so we need to come into this and somehow add support for arena-based allocations, and if these swaps end up needing to copy for any reason, having a way of doing that with an arena to save on allocation overhead. And so when we implemented arenas, it ended up adding a whole lot of code, a whole lot of code. And there are a couple of different reasons why we had to add this much code. The first one is that
cues.zh: 因此我们需要介入这里，想办法加入对基于 arena 内存分配的支持，如果这些交换出于某些原因最终需要复制，也能有一种利用 arena 来做的方式，从而节省内存分配开销。因此当我们实现 arena 时，最终增加了大量的代码，真的是非常多的代码。我们不得不增加这么多代码，有几个不同的原因。第一个原因在于

cues.en: we can't be certain that all of these protocol buffers have been allocated on an arena. And even worse, we can't be certain that they've been allocated on the same arena. And so when we add arena support, we have to test for all of these different conditions to know if it's safe for us to actually use the arena-based swap implementation. And it turns out those tests are really, really expensive, okay?
cues.zh: 我们无法确定所有这些 Protocol Buffers 都分配在 arena 上。更糟的是，也无法确定它们是在同一个 arena 上分配的。所以加入 arena 支持时，我们必须测试所有这些不同情况，才能知道是否可以安全地使用基于 arena 的 swap 实现。而结果发现，这些测试真的非常非常昂贵，明白吗？

cues.en: And so we put them in these inline functions in our generated header files to make sure they could get inlined every single place that they're used. The optimizer can remove this runtime overhead of this abstraction, but it wasn't enough. And so we generated an extra method, the unsafe swap. And then we taught other parts of the code generator to generate direct calls to that to skip these extra checks. And we kept using this code generator abstraction to solve our runtime problems.
cues.zh: 所以我们把它们放进了生成的头文件中的这些内联函数里，以确保在每个使用的地方都能被内联。优化器可以消除这种抽象带来的运行时开销，但这还不够。所以我们额外生成了一个方法：unsafe swap。然后我们让代码生成器的其他部分直接生成对它的调用，从而跳过这些额外的检查。而且我们一直在用这种代码生成器抽象来解决我们的运行时问题。

cues.en: because we wanted this abstraction to be a zero-cost abstraction. It makes sense. This is in the critical path of every Google server. All of these movements are incredibly expensive. But by the time we finished it, this is a complex change. The change from not having the arenas to having the arenas is a really complex change to the code. We don't want it just like...
cues.zh: 因为我们希望这种抽象成为一种零成本抽象。这很合理。这处于每个 Google 服务器的关键路径上。所有这些数据移动都极其昂贵。但当我们完成它时，发现这是一项复杂的改动。从不使用 arena 到使用 arena，对代码来说是一个非常复杂的改动。我们不想让它只是……

cues.en: Throw a big switch and turn it on everywhere. At Google, we have an enormous code base, hundreds of millions of lines of C++ code. We don't want to change all of our servers in one fell swoop. So we made this opt-in. You add a little flag to your protocol buffer message, and it says, hey, I want to use arenas to allocate my protocol buffers. And you get this extra logic, which is great. This means we have a nice incremental rollout. So sometime in the late...
cues.zh: 直接拨动大开关，在所有地方全量开启。在 Google，我们有极其庞大的代码库，数亿行 C++ 代码。我们不想一下子把所有服务器全改了。所以我们做成了可选开启。你只要在 protocol buffer message 里加一个小标志，声明“嘿，我想用 arena 来分配我的 protocol buffer”。然后就能获得这个额外逻辑，这棒极了。这意味着我们可以很好地渐进式发布。于是在差不多...

cues.en: 2013, teams started rolling this out to all of the most important protocol buffer messages in our code base. And it was really easy to do. They just added this one line of code, so they were able to roll it out pretty quickly, even though it was incremental. But we noticed something as that was going on. We have monitoring for our compile times, and they weren't going in the shape that we wanted. And so the red line at the bottom here is the average compile time.
cues.zh: 2013 年底，各个团队开始把这推广到代码库中所有最重要的 protocol buffer message 上。这做起来非常简单。他们只需要加上这一行代码，所以即便它是增量的，大家也能相当迅速地铺开。但随着推进，我们发现了一些苗头。我们对编译时间做了监控，而它们的走向并不是我们想要的。底部这里的红线代表平均编译时间，

cues.en: for a single file in our distributed build system, in our entire code base. The green line is the 90th percentile, and the blue line at the top is the 99th percentile. And you'll notice in late 2013, these lines start bending upwards much more rapidly. I mean, it wasn't really good before that, but it got a lot worse in late 2013, and as we got into early 2014, the situation became really dire, okay?
cues.zh: 是全代码库中单个文件在我们分布式构建系统里的耗时。绿线是第 90 百分位数，最上面的蓝线是第 99 百分位数。大家会注意到在 2013 年底，这些折线开始更快地往上蹿。我是说，在那之前情况本来就一般，但到了 2013 年底就糟糕多了；等进入 2014 年初，情况变得极其严峻，对吧？

cues.en: And to understand how bad this is, you have to think about what a build actually looks like. We build all of our software from source, and so if you're building a large C++ application, you might compile hundreds, thousands, even tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of source files in a single build. And if the 90th percentile is starting to trend upward in a dangerous way, then...
cues.zh: 要想明白这有多糟糕，你得想想一次构建实际上是什么样的。我们所有的软件都是从源码编译构建的，所以如果你在构建一个大型 C++ 应用，单次构建中你可能要编译几百、几千，甚至是几万或几十万个源文件。如果第 90 百分位数开始危险地上升，那么……

cues.en: you definitely have a large number of compiles in one build that are in the 90th percentile, because you're compiling 100,000 files. In fact, the 99th percentile is also in every single build, okay? And so, despite the fact that we think this is rare, in fact, every single developer at Google was hitting the 99th percentile case somewhere.
